answer.rationale:
Constraints dominate: the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days, so any action that interrupts flow is disqualified regardless of unit-cost upside. That rules out switch_primary_vendor this cycle (memory_c2 reports a fast, clean onboarding, but the record is a consolidated summary that does not say whether it covered this constrained component, at what share of volume, or what qualification lead time was consumed \u2014 14 days is almost certainly inside that window). defer_decision is also out: the contract does not auto-renew, so deferral is not a neutral hold, it is an unpriced supply gap. Plain renew_incumbent is safe on delivery but concedes the 18% mandate entirely.

That leaves negotiate_terms as the one decision that can serve both objectives. The incumbent refused to reopen *price* this cycle, but memory_c6 describes a different lever \u2014 term length traded for volume pricing, with service scope intact \u2014 which is not the same ask as a mid-cycle price reopen. memory_c4 independently shows this incumbent moves when benchmarked against market rates, and memory_c2 supplies exactly that benchmark as negotiating leverage even if we do not execute the switch.

I want the two archived records because both load-bearing memories could be misleading in ways the summaries hide. memory_c6: I need to know whether the volume discount required a genuine multi-year lock and what the actual realized unit-cost delta was, because if the discount is thin it will not approach 18% and I am buying lock-in for little. memory_c2: I need the qualification timeline and the component scope, both to price the threat credibly and to know whether a second source is viable next cycle. I did not pull memory_c3, though dual-sourcing is the right structural answer to the no-buffer problem \u2014 it simply cannot be stood up inside 14 days and belongs in the next review.

Guarded scale is deliberate. The strongest version of the memory_c6 play is a long multi-year commitment, and that is precisely what I want to avoid signing: locking multiple years now forecloses the dual-source and switch options at the exact moment an unverified low-cost alternative exists and a hard cost mandate is in force. So I target the shortest term that unlocks tiered pricing, with scope and service levels held explicit in writing.

Downstream risk flagged on two counts. First, an 18% cut extracted from a supplier who has already refused on price will tend to be recovered somewhere \u2014 quality tolerances, expedite responsiveness, allocation priority in the next shortage \u2014 none of which appear in a unit-cost metric until the line stops. Second, all six memories are consolidated summaries whose sources are archived; they record what worked without recording base rates or the conditions that made it work, and c6 in particular predates the incumbent's current refusal posture. Uncertainty preserved: if the archive shows the volume discount is small or requires a term longer than I will accept, the fallback is a short bridge renewal at current terms plus immediate second-source qualification next cycle, not a forced switch into a line with no buffer.
